items.title: The oxygen you breathe comes from WATER, not CO2
items.claim: Photosynthesis takes in CO2 and water and produces sugar and oxygen. Every chemistry student writes the equation. But the O2 released is not stripped from the CO2 — it comes entirely from splitting water molecules.
items.prompt: How do we know the oxygen comes from water?

options.text: Both water and CO2 contribute oxygen equally
Ruben and Kamen (1941) used the heavy isotope oxygen-18 to label either water or CO2; the released O2 carried the label only when the water was labelled, never when the CO2 was
CO2 is the source of the oxygen

items.reveal:
The light reactions of photosynthesis split water (photolysis) at the oxygen-evolving complex — a manganese-calcium cluster in Photosystem II. Two water molecules are split: 2 H2O -> 4 H+ + 4 e- + O2.

The electrons enter the electron transport chain. The protons contribute to the thylakoid pH gradient (lumen reaches pH ~5, stroma ~8). ATP synthase uses the gradient to make ATP.

The Calvin cycle (in the stroma) uses ATP and NADPH to fix CO2 into sugar. The carbon from CO2 becomes the carbon in glucose. But the oxygen atoms in CO2 mostly end up in carbohydrate, NOT in the released O2.

Oxygen is, from photosynthesis's point of view, a waste product — and arguably the most consequential pollution event in Earth's history (the Great Oxidation Event, ~2.4 billion years ago, killed most anaerobic life).
items.why: The arrow-pushing equation suggests CO2 donates oxygen. The actual chemistry inverts that: water is split, CO2 is reduced, and the oxygen you breathe was once dissolved in a chloroplast.

items.title: Babies have a special fat that wastes energy as heat — on purpose
items.claim: Brown adipose tissue, found in newborns and hibernating mammals, contains mitochondria packed with a protein (UCP1) that lets protons leak back across the inner membrane WITHOUT making ATP. The energy is dissipated as pure heat.
items.prompt: Why deliberately uncouple respiration from ATP synthesis?

options.text: It's a mistake the body cannot fix
Newborns and small mammals lose heat fast (high surface area to volume ratio). Brown fat lets them generate large amounts of heat on demand without shivering — burning fat directly to warmth

items.reveal:
In ordinary mitochondria, the electron transport chain pumps protons OUT; ATP synthase lets them back IN, capturing the energy as ATP.

In brown adipose tissue, the protein UCP1 (uncoupling protein 1, also called thermogenin) provides an alternative route for protons to flow back in — bypassing ATP synthase. The proton gradient still forms; the energy still flows; but it dissipates as heat rather than ATP.

Brown fat is brown because it's packed with mitochondria (iron-rich cytochromes). It's especially abundant in newborn humans (around the neck and shoulder blades) and in hibernating mammals (which use it to wake from torpor).

Adults retain some brown fat, more in lean people; PET-CT scans light it up. There's active research into pharmacologically activating brown fat as an anti-obesity strategy.

The drug DNP (2,4-dinitrophenol) chemically uncouples mitochondria. It does cause weight loss — but also fatal hyperthermia. It's been banned for human use for nearly a century, though it still kills bodybuilders occasionally.
items.why: Inefficiency seems like a flaw. The body uses controlled mitochondrial inefficiency as a thermostat — and biotech is trying to weaponise it against obesity.

items.title: A tumour is a tiny evolving ecosystem
items.claim: Cancer cells accumulate mutations. Cells with mutations that confer growth advantages dominate. Drug treatment kills the susceptible cells but spares resistant ones — which then dominate the regrown tumour.
items.prompt: Why is cancer so hard to cure even with effective drugs?

options.text: Drugs don't work on cancer cells

A tumour contains millions to billions of slightly genetically different cells; selection pressure from a drug acts on the existing variation and rapidly enriches resistant clones — the same evolutionary process as antibiotic resistance, but inside a single patient

items.reveal_title: Tumour heterogeneity and the cost of monotherapy
items.reveal:
Single-cell sequencing of tumours reveals enormous clonal diversity. A 5 cm tumour may contain 10 to the 9 cells, each with its own profile of acquired mutations. Subclones can have different drug sensitivities, growth rates and metastatic potentials.

Treating with a single targeted therapy selects for whichever cells are pre-existingly resistant. Within months, the tumour regrows — now dominated by the resistant subclone. Combination therapy (targeting multiple pathways at once) makes resistance much less likely, by analogy with HIV's HAART protocol.

The Peter Nowell paper (1976) first proposed clonal evolution in cancer. Recent decades have made it the dominant framework, with implications for drug strategy, biomarker design, and the inevitability of resistance.
items.why: Cancer is taught as one disease. It's an evolving population of cells subject to selection — making it as much an ecological and evolutionary problem as a medical one.
